problem: The answer says a '50–70 % margin' and that operating at 50–70 % of the flooding rate 'keeps the bed below loading'. The margin below flooding is 30–50 %, not 50–70 %; and the loading point typically sits around 65–85 % of the flooding gas rate, so a design point at 70 % of flooding can be at or above loading. A student will carry both errors into the exam.
fix: Operating at 50–70 % of the flooding gas mass flux leaves a 30–50 % margin below flooding, so small upsets in gas or liquid rate do not push the bed into flooding. Pressure drop stays modest, and the design point is normally kept at or below the loading point. Flooding itself is unstable: liquid is held up and blown back.

problem: The sentence 'A 25 mm ring has a near 200 m²/m³, not 25 m²/m³' reads badly: the symbol a is used as an English word and the sentence can be misread.
fix: A 25 mm ring has a specific surface of about 200 m²/m³, not 25 m²/m³.

where: Section 1, definition of a (and Quiz Q1 answer)
problem: a is defined as the 'wetted area' of packing per unit volume of bed, then used as a fixed geometric property of the packing. The standard definition is the total surface area of the packing per unit volume of bed; the wetted area equals it only when the liquid covers the whole surface.
fix: Specific surface a is the surface area of the packing per unit volume of packed bed, in m²/m³. The wetted area, which is what actually transfers solute, is at most this value and falls below it when liquid channels or the packing is not fully wet.

where: Section 1, bullet on size and void fraction
problem: The statement that ε usually lies between 0.6 and 0.95 is too tight: gauze packings and the more open structured sheet packings reach about 0.95–0.98, and the chapter's own later discussion of structured packings expects high voidage.
fix: ε usually lies between 0.6 and 0.95 for random packings and ordinary structured sheet packings; wire-gauze and very open structured packings reach about 0.95–0.98.
